opening_line: Explaining shared hosting as the inner tube jam just past Barber Park on a July float is something a Boise client will actually remember. Saving twenty bucks a month to sit in that jam gets hard to defend.
You wrote that a logo is the invitation and the website is the room people walk into. A fair share of logo-only clients probably come back to you for the room.
You wrote that ecommerce isn't something you advertise and that Elo Coffee was the exception that fit. Saying no to the wrong builds is probably what keeps a small studio's calendar sane.

You took IBM's 2026 CEO study, written for the Fortune 500, and turned it into plays for a five-person service business in Bend. Clients who read that probably show up wanting a lot more than a new website.

Your point that people land on a municipal site to pay a utility bill or check garbage day, not to read about the brand, applies well beyond towns. Organizing hundreds of pages around tasks is a lot of design work.

"The redirect map matters more than the mockups" is a hard sentence for most designers to accept, and the roofing URL example shows why. Fixing a redesign that lost its rankings is usually rushed work for whoever gets the call.

Your line about publishing better evidence instead of more pages, now that AI made pages cheap, changes what a trades site is. Pages built from real jobs and crawlspace finds take a lot more design time than templates.

You wrote that a CFO or a city procurement committee reads an AEC firm's website as evidence of who they are. That puts a lot of weight on design for clients who usually treat the site as an afterthought.
The dark green panel with that italic serif, set over a full bleed wildlife photo, gives The Wildlife Society a front page that looks like a field journal.
